sections.title: Indian Economy: Agriculture, Trading Networks, and Merchant Communities

slides.title: Jats Under Mughal Pressure
slides.kicker: Farmers of the Doab had enough
bullets: The Jats were a farming community from the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
In the 17th century they carried heavy taxes and exploitation by the Mughals.
Aurangzeb's religious policies added to the economic hardships and growing resentment.
slides.note: Taxes on the crop, hurt in the heart — kisan ki patience ran out.

slides.title: 1669: Gokul Jat Rises
slides.kicker: One leader, months of Mughal struggle
bullets: In 1669 the Jats rebelled against the Mughal Empire under the leadership of Gokul Jat.
Mughal forces struggled for many months to suppress the uprising.
Even after this first revolt was checked, the Jats continued their resistance.
slides.note: Revolt number one: the empire needed months, not weeks.

slides.title: 1686: The Second Uprising
slides.kicker: While Aurangzeb was busy in the Deccan
bullets: In 1686 the Jats rebelled again under the leadership of the zamindars of Sinsani and Sogar.
They took advantage of Aurangzeb's prolonged military campaigns in the Deccan.
The Mughals sent several armies; both sides suffered heavy losses in a long fierce struggle.
By 1691 the Mughals had gained the upper hand, yet the Jat resistance continued.
slides.note: Timing matters: a distracted emperor weakens far away.

slides.title: An Italian Records the Jats
bullets: Niccolao Manucci, an Italian traveller, journeyed through 17th century India.
He wrote an extensive account of India, including descriptions of Jat resistance against the Mughals.
A traveller's record lets us see the Jat struggle from close quarters.
slides.note: A traveller's pen can outlast an empire's army.

slides.title: A Devotional Wave Rises
slides.kicker: Bhakti swept India for ten centuries
bullets: Between the 11th and 17th centuries India's religious and spiritual landscape was profoundly transformed.
Bhakti is a tradition of personal devotion to the divine, expressed through hymns composed in local languages.
From the 7th century onwards, Bhakti rose and expanded in peninsular India, shaping social, religious and political life.
slides.note: Devotion sung in your own tongue — that is Bhakti.

slides.title: Saints of the People
bullets: Bhakti emphasised inclusivity, socio-religious equality, simplicity and connecting with everyday life.
Eknath composed in Marathi and offered a devotional path accessible to all, without dependence on institutions.
Nayanar saints like Karaikal Ammaiyar (devotees of Shiva) and Alvar saints like Andal (devotees of Vishnu) spread Bhakti through hymns.
slides.note: No gatekeepers here — devotion opened for everyone.

slides.title: Two Streams of Bhakti
slides.kicker: Formless divine, or divine with attributes
bullets: From the 14th century onwards a strong wave of Bhakti spread across northern India.
Ramananda, a prominent saint of this period, helped bridge the Bhakti traditions of southern and northern India.
Nirguna bhakti was devoted to a formless divine; Saguna bhakti centred on a divine with attributes.
A remarkable feature was the diverse social and cultural background of the Bhakti saints.

right.title: Saguna bhakti
items: centred on a divine with attributes

slides.note: One wave, two ways of imagining the divine.

slides.title: Faith Too Mobile to Crush
slides.kicker: When temples fell, songs carried on
bullets: When temple construction faced restrictions or temples were destroyed, devotees turned to nam kirtan, the recitation of the divine Name.
This nonmaterial worship depended less on physical structures that could be destroyed.
Local songs and community participation (satsang) made Bhakti accessible to wider sections of society and hard to suppress.
Sankardev composed the Kirtana Ghosha, a highly respected work that remains central to this day.
slides.note: You can break stone, but not a song on every lip.

slides.title: Temples Ran the Economy
bullets: Temples functioned as central pillars of the region's socio-economic and political life.
They managed extensive land grants, employed hundreds of specialised workers and served as financial institutions for local traders.
Temples exercised quasi-judicial authority, collecting local taxes and administering legal penalties.
As centres of education and culture they preserved artistic traditions such as Bharatanatyam.
slides.note: A temple could be bank, court, school and stage at once.

slides.title: Kings as Deputies
slides.kicker: When the deity was the real ruler
bullets: The deities of temples were regarded as protectors of the state and its people.
In some cases the deity was regarded as the ruler, while the actual ruler governed as the deity's deputy.
The Gajapati rulers of Odisha called themselves the Rauta (deputy) of Jagannath.
The Kachhwaha rulers of Jaipur governed on behalf of Govindadevaji; the Rajput rulers of Kota saw themselves as representatives of Rama.

children: Gajapati of Odisha: Rauta of Jagannath
Rajputs of Kota: representatives of Rama

slides.note: A quiet source of legitimacy: rule in the god's name.

slides.title: Gold, Credit, Temple Towns
slides.kicker: Donations flowed in, loans flowed out
bullets: Temples received donations, endowments and land grants, often given as acts of religious merit.
The Brihadeeswara (Rajarajeshvara) temple at Thanjavur received extensive donations of gold, ornaments and vessels.
Temple wealth supported irrigation works and agrarian development; credit went to cultivators, village assemblies and merchant groups.
This convergence helped temple towns like Thanjavur, Kanchipuram and Puri emerge as prominent urban centres.
slides.note: Follow the gold: it watered fields and raised cities.

slides.title: Patronage, Then Destruction
bullets: Between the 7th and 13th centuries temple construction proliferated across the subcontinent under the patronage of various dynasties.
From the 11th century onwards, many instances of temple destruction occurred, particularly during the Ghaznavid and Ghurid invasions.
From the 12th century onwards, many temples and maths were also affected.
Rulers used temple patronage to strengthen their political legitimacy.
slides.note: Wealthy temples were both pride and target.

slides.title: Land Revenue Powers States
bullets: The early second millennium CE saw the agrarian economy expand and centres of artisanal and craft production proliferate.
Land revenue was the main source of state income.
Expanding frontiers of empires resulted in an increase in the area under cultivation.
Over time, land revenue collection became increasingly strict and exploitative at various levels of administration.
slides.note: More fields, more tax — kisan ka jhuka sar aur bhari.

slides.title: Half the Harvest as Tax
bullets: Under Alauddin Khilji and Mohammad bin Tughlaq the land tax rose to as much as 50 per cent of total agricultural production.
This land tax was in addition to other taxes.
Sultans of Delhi and later Mughals had a limited role in maritime trade, mostly political, military and customs matters.
Coastal areas and their commerce remained largely in the hands of regional power holders and local communities.
slides.note: The court took half the crop; the coastline kept its freedom.

slides.title: Water Works, Bigger Harvests
bullets: Technologies like the rope pulley, spinning wheel and Persian wheel were widely used, enhancing agricultural and economic output.
In the Vijayanagara Empire, agricultural production varied greatly in both form and scale.
Irrigation there ranged from extensive canal networks to small rain-fed patches of land.
A defining feature of the Vijayanagara economy was its investment in small-scale irrigation.

right.title: Small rain-fed patches
items: the other end of the range

slides.note: Smart small works beat no works at all.

slides.title: Hundi: Paper Instead of Bullion
slides.kicker: The cheque of the second millennium
bullets: Trade grew in this era, and India's inland regions were connected to trade routes in Central Asia.
Hundi, a financial instrument compared in some respects to modern bank cheques, was widely used.
It worked as a bill of exchange, enabling large-scale transactions without carrying large amounts of currency.
Hundis gave secured long-distance remittance through sarrafs, the money-changers, and their agents called gumasthas.

items: trader deposits money with a sarraf
hundi issued as a bill of exchange

slides.note: Send paper, not silver — safer on lonely roads.

slides.title: The Chapter's Big Idea
bullets: The key MCQ idea: resistance and resilience connect because resilience enables communities to endure difficulties and sustain resistance.
Other questions ask why the Sikhs, Marathas and Rajputs asserted their political power and identity in changing times.
One question explores why some Rajput rulers chose to negotiate alliances with Mughal power.
slides.note: Endure first, resist longer — that is the pairing.

slides.title: Traders, Ports and Forts
bullets: One activity imagines a market in port towns like Surat, Masulipatnam or Puducherry.
You play a foreign trader from Italy or France buying cotton textiles, facing challenges of language, quality and prices.
Another asks how rulers perceived the strategic importance of forts, using the Tales of Forts videos on indianculture.gov.in.
A question links architectural changes in temple construction to the resilient nature of Indian civilisation.
slides.note: Haggle hard, foreigner — the bazaar teaches history.

slides.title: Voices and Fort Design
bullets: Voices from the Past: write accounts as a Bhakti saint, Rajput soldier, Ahom commander, Maratha administrator, merchant or Jat leader.
Design a Fort: plan walls, water source, food storage, escape route, watchtower, residential complex and administrative area.
A statement to debate: a tradition becomes more resilient when people can carry it with them.
A scenario asks how fertile land, local support and terrain knowledge build a kingdom's resilience.
slides.note: Draw the fort, then argue like a saint.

examples.title: Chronology of the Jat resistance
examples.problem: Arrange the Jat resistance against the Mughals into a clear timeline, and state what each stage shows about resilience.
steps: 17th century: the Jats of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab face heavy taxes, exploitation and Aurangzeb's religious policies.
1669: Gokul Jat leads the first rebellion; Mughal forces struggle for many months to suppress it.
1686: the zamindars of Sinsani and Sogar lead a second rising, using Aurangzeb's absence in prolonged Deccan campaigns.
1686 to 1691: several Mughal armies fight a long fierce struggle; both sides suffer heavy losses.
1691: the Mughals gain the upper hand, yet the Jat resistance continues.
examples.answer: 1669 first rising under Gokul Jat; 1686 second rising under the zamindars of Sinsani and Sogar; by 1691 the Mughals held the upper hand, but the resistance continued — endurance itself was the Jats' resilience.

examples.title: Sorting the Bhakti streams
examples.problem: Classify each of the following: devotion to a formless divine, devotion to a divine with attributes, Ramananda, and hymns in local languages.
steps: Recall the definitions: Nirguna bhakti is devoted to a formless divine; Saguna bhakti is centred on a divine with attributes.
Place devotion to a formless divine in the Nirguna stream.
Place devotion to a divine with attributes in the Saguna stream.
Place Ramananda as the prominent 14th century saint who bridged the Bhakti traditions of southern and northern India.
Note that both streams used devotional hymns composed in local languages, so local-language hymns belong to the whole tradition.
examples.answer: Nirguna: the formless divine. Saguna: the divine with attributes. Ramananda: the bridge between southern and northern Bhakti. Hymns in local languages: common to the entire Bhakti wave.

examples.title: Following temple wealth to temple towns
examples.problem: Trace how a great temple like the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur turned donations into urban growth.
steps: Devotees and rulers gave donations, endowments and land grants as acts of religious merit; the Brihadeeswara temple received gold, ornaments and vessels.
As substantial landholders, temples employed architects, artisans, sculptors, priests, musicians and administrative staff.
Temple wealth supported irrigation works and agrarian development.
Temples extended credit to cultivators, village assemblies and merchant groups.
This convergence of economic and religious activity made temple towns like Thanjavur, Kanchipuram and Puri prominent urban centres.
examples.answer: Donations became employment, irrigation and credit; that economic muscle turned Thanjavur, Kanchipuram and Puri into prominent temple towns.

examples.title: A merchant sends money by hundi
examples.problem: A trader must send the payment for a large consignment of cotton textiles to a distant partner without carrying currency on the road. Using the book's description, show how a hundi completes the payment.
steps: The trader goes to a sarraf, a money-changer, instead of loading a chest of coins.
The sarraf issues a hundi, a bill of exchange comparable in some respects to a modern bank cheque.
The hundi travels through the sarraf's agents, the gumasthas, who operate the network.
The partner presents the hundi and receives the money, a trusted means of secured long-distance remittance.
The deal settles without carrying large amounts of currency, which is why hundis suited large-scale commercial transactions.
examples.answer: Deposit with a sarraf, hundi issued as a bill of exchange, gumastha network transfers the claim, partner collects the cash at the far end — no bullion on the road.
